identity.title: Stellar feedback in M83 as observed with MUSE. I. Overview, an unprecedented view of the stellar and gas kinematics and evidence of outflowing gas

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present a large mosaic (3.8 $\times$ 3.8 kpc) of the nearby spiral galaxy M83, obtained with the MUSE instrument at ESO Very Large Telescope (VLT).
We obtained the kinematics of the stars and ionised gas, and compared them with molecular gas kinematics observed in CO(2-1) with the ALMA telescope array.

question.value: How do the kinematics of stars, ionised gas, and molecular gas compare in M83 at ~20 pc scales, and what is the fraction and ionisation mechanism of diffuse ionised gas and central outflow/inflow structures?

evidence.quote: We obtained the kinematics of the stars and ionised gas, and compared them with molecular gas kinematics observed in CO(2-1) with the ALMA telescope array.

We separated the ionised gas into H ii regions and diffuse ionised gas (DIG) and investigated how the fraction of H$\alpha$ luminosity originating from the DIG ($f_{\rm DIG}$) varies with galactic radius.
Ultimately, we aim to provide a comprehensive picture of the star formation cycle in M83 at tens of parsec scales.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive stellar, ionised gas, and molecular gas kinematics and fit 2D rotation models

method.value: Voronoi binning and PPXF fitting for stellar continuum; single and double Gaussian fitting (with BIC selection) for H-alpha in continuum-subtracted cube; PHANGS-ALMA mom1/mom2 maps and Gaussian fits to CO spectra; 2D double-Plummer rotation curve fitting with MocKinG

evidence.quote: We fitted the stellar continuum with PPXF (cite: cappellari04; cappellari17), using the E-MILES simple stellar populations models (cite: vazdekis16) with an unimodal IMF and Padova 2000 isochrones (cite: girardi00).
We Voronoi binned the gas cube to a S/N $\sim$ 20 in H$\alpha$[^5] and fitted the line with a single Gaussian profile.

In order to derive the global kinematic parameters of M83, we fitted the velocity maps of stars and gas with the 2D fitting method described in (cite: epinat08) and based on the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear least-square algorithm. In our work, the method has been upgraded using the MocKinG software[^6] to take into account uncertainties on the line of sight (LoS) velocities, the flux distribution, the linewidth of the profiles and the spatial resolution.

key_parameters.value: Stellar Voronoi S/N ~ 250 in 5025-5065 A, fit range 4600-8740 A (excluding 7220-8507 A)

evidence.quote: The bins were targeted to a signal to noise ratio (S/N) $\simeq$ 250 in the continuum range 5025 – 5065 Å, corresponding to a S/N $\simeq$ 40 Å$^{-1}$. We fitted the range 4600 – 8740 Å (in order to include the Ca ii triplet).
in particular, we excluded entirely the range 7220 – 8507 Å due to the strong residual sky emission.

findings_qualitative.value: Both stars and gas trace regular disk rotation as well as a fast-rotating circumnuclear disk (~30'' or 700 pc in diameter).

evidence.quote: We observe that both stars and gas trace the galactic disk rotation, as well as a fast-rotating nuclear component (30$''$ $\simeq$ 700 pc in diameter), likely connected to secular processes driven by the galactic bar.

findings_qualitative.value: East of the nucleus, a redshifted stream (feature C, 50'' or 1250 pc) is seen in both H-alpha (+30 km s^-1) and ALMA CO(2-1) (multiple peaks with one redshifted by +100 km s^-1), surrounded by a 1000 x 1600 pc region with high velocity dispersion and slow-shock ionisation.

evidence.quote: On top of the disk rotation, the gas traces a flow east of the nucleus (50$''$ $\simeq$ 1250 pc in size), that appears redshifted on top of the disk rotation. In the ionised gas, we observe $\Delta v_{\rm H\alpha} \simeq$ +30 km s$^{-1}$ with respect to the surroundings, and in the molecular gas we observe multiple peaks of emission, one of which is redshifted by $\Delta v_{\rm CO} \simeq$ +100 km s$^{-1}$ with respect to the emission tracing galactic rotation.

findings_qualitative.value: A double-Gaussian fit to H-alpha reveals a nuclear biconic outflow structure (cones A and B, ~500 pc in size) perpendicular to the bar with velocity separations up to 200 km s^-1 and shock signatures at the far ends.

evidence.quote: A double Gaussian component fit to the H$\alpha$ line also reveals the presence of a nuclear biconic structure whose axis of symmetry is perpendicular to the bar. The two cones (20$''$ $\simeq$ 500 pc in size) appear blue- and redshifted along the line of sight.

findings_qualitative.value: Regions with high ionised gas extinction (E(B-V) > 0.5) correspond closely to dense molecular gas (> 100 M_sun pc^-2) traced by ALMA CO(2-1), except in the southern circumnuclear peak due to vertical geometry along the line of sight.

evidence.loc: Extinction traced by the molecular and ionised gas
evidence.quote: By comparing the extinction map with the CO intensity emission traced by ALMA (left panels in Fig. [5](#fig:ebv_map)), we observe that indeed regions with high extinction correspond to dense molecular gas, with a surface density larger than $100~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$ pc$^{-2}$ (black contours in the top right panel Fig. [5](#fig:ebv_map)).

evidence.loc: Extinction traced by the molecular and ionised gas
evidence.quote: The southern CO peak (receding part of the circumnuclear disk) shows very low extinction values. Given the inclination of the galaxy, we interpret this as a perspective effect on the vertical separation of the gas, due to the denser molecular gas residing deeper in the disk: the low extinction traced by the ionised gas would then be estimated based on line ratios from gas that is on top of the CO layer.

claims.hypothesis: The nuclear biconic H-alpha structures (cones A and B) trace a starburst-driven outflow shocking into the surrounding ISM.
claims.experiment: Perform double-component Gaussian fitting to H-alpha and other optical emission lines in the central starburst region, and evaluate BPT line ratios and shock-sensitive ratios ([O III]/H-alpha, [O I]/H-alpha).
claims.result: Two cones (20'' ~ 500 pc) perpendicular to the bar show velocity separations up to 200 km s^-1, dispersions of 80-200 km s^-1, and line ratios at d >= 20'' consistent with slow shock models.
claims.finding: The cones trace a starburst-driven outflow perpendicular to the stellar bar that shocks into the surrounding ISM at its far ends.

evidence.quote: The cones stand out for having an H$\alpha$ emission separated by up to 200 km s$^{-1}$ from that of the disk, and a high velocity dispersion $\sim$ 80 – 200 km s$^{-1}$. At the far end of the cones, we observe that the gas is consistent with being ionised by shocks. These features had never been observed before in M83; we postulate that they are tracing a starburst-driven outflow shocking into the surrounding ISM.

claims.hypothesis: The redshifted stream east of the nucleus (feature C) and its surrounding high-dispersion region represent either a superposition of disk and extraplanar DIG or a bar-driven inflow of shocked gas.
claims.experiment: Compare MUSE H-alpha kinematics and BPT shock diagnostics with ALMA CO(2-1) kinematics and spectra across feature C.
claims.result: Feature C shows H-alpha redshifted by +30 km s^-1 surrounded by a 1000 x 1600 pc slow-shocked region with sigma ~ 80 km s^-1, while ALMA CO(2-1) shows multiple velocity peaks with a component redshifted by ~100 km s^-1 and mass 4e6 M_sun.
claims.finding: Feature C is consistent with either the superposition of the disk and an extraplanar layer of gas or a bar-driven inflow of shocked gas.

evidence.quote: The stream is surrounded by an extended ionised gas region (1000 $\times$ 1600 pc) with enhanced velocity dispersion and a high ionisation state, which is largely consistent with being ionised by slow shocks. We interpret this feature as either the superposition of the disk and an extraplanar layer of DIG, or as a bar-driven inflow of shocked gas.

In the ionised gas, we observe $\Delta v_{\rm H\alpha} \simeq$ +30 km s$^{-1}$ with respect to the surroundings, and in the molecular gas we observe multiple peaks of emission, one of which is redshifted by $\Delta v_{\rm CO} \simeq$ +100 km s$^{-1}$ with respect to the emission tracing galactic rotation.

claims.hypothesis: The diffuse ionised gas (DIG) in the inner disk of M83 is predominantly ionised by radiation leaking from star-forming regions, with a minor contribution from shocks.
claims.experiment: Separate H II regions and DIG using ASTRODENDRO and [S II]/H-alpha cuts, measure the radial profile of f_DIG, and classify Voronoi bins in BPT diagrams.
claims.result: f_DIG is ~13% (20% with [S II]/H-alpha cut) overall and varies radially from 0.8% to 46%; 94.9% of DIG H-alpha flux lies in the photoionisation regime and 5.1% in the shock regime.
claims.finding: The DIG in the inner disk is mainly ionised by photons escaping star-forming regions, with a 5.1% contribution from shocks.

evidence.quote: Finally, we obtain $f_{\rm DIG} \sim$ 13% in our field of view, and observe that the DIG contribution varies radially between 0.8 and 46%, peaking in the interarm region. We inspect the emission of the H ii regions and DIG in ‘BPT’ diagrams, finding that in H ii regions photoionisation accounts for 99.8% of the H$\alpha$ flux, whereas the DIG has a mixed contribution from photoionisation (94.9%) and shocks (5.1%).

why_this_data.value: MUSE wide-field IFS mosaic at ~20 pc resolution bridges 10 pc and kpc scales across diverse galactic environments, while archival ALMA CO(2-1) traces the molecular gas distribution and kinematics.

evidence.quote: Our work complements the very high resolution (10 pc) studies and the large scale (100 pc – kpc) studies, by covering a wide area ($\sim$ 20 arcmin$^2$) at a resolution that still allows the characterisation of individual H ii regions while at the same time sampling a large number of regions ($\sim 4700$, Della Bruna et al., in prep) and a wide range of ISM conditions across the galactic disk.
At the same time, the HST coverage provides us with a detailed catalogue of massive stars and clusters, and the ALMA data trace the distribution of the molecular gas in the galaxy.

why_this_method.value: Double Gaussian fitting with BIC selection captures unresolved line broadening and double-peaked outflow profiles without overfitting; 2D double-Plummer fitting handles both the disk and steep central component.

evidence.quote: A double component can better capture the emission in the case of extreme line broadening on top of a single emission line peak (caused e.g. by shocks or unresolved flows) and in the case where the line has a double-peaked profile, tracing gas motions on top of the galactic rotation (e.g. resolved flows).

evidence.loc: Analysis of the stellar velocity field
evidence.quote: The Plummer density profile has a finite density core and falls off as $r^{-5}$ at large radii; this very steep fall-off was essential to fit at best the central component.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Past galaxy interaction (e.g., with NGC 5253) as the origin of feature C and central kinematic peculiarities, rejected due to the regular stellar rotation field.

evidence.loc: Kinematic features in the starburst region
evidence.quote: A final possibility could be a past interaction, possibly with the neighbouring galaxy NGC 5253 (1.8$^\circ$ in projected distance).

evidence.loc: Kinematic features in the starburst region
evidence.quote: However, given the extremely regular stellar rotation field and the general lack of global scale perturbances, we discard this hypothesis.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: AGN-driven outflow or superposition of bar-driven orbits as the sole explanation for cones A and B, disfavoured compared to a starburst-driven outflow.

evidence.loc: Kinematic features in the starburst region
evidence.quote: Given the fact that the origin of cones A and B is offset from the galaxy’s centre, the lack of shock-related emission immediately surrounding the central region and the presence of slow shocks, we favour over the presence of an AGN the hypothesis of a starburst-driven outflow cone shocking into the surrounding ISM.

evidence.loc: Kinematic features in the starburst region
evidence.quote: Finally, what appear as redshifted and blueshifted cones along our line of sight could simply simply be the result of the superposition of bar-driven orbits, resulting from the non-axisymmetric and time varying potential. However, this effect alone would be difficult to reconcile with the large separation between the two peaks of H$\alpha$ emission (up to 200 km s$^{-1}$) at the centre of the cones.

limitations_admitted.value: Velocity dispersions below ~50 km s^-1 at H-alpha are undersampled by the MUSE instrumental LSF.

evidence.quote: We note that following this parametrisation, velocity dispersions below $\sim$ 50 km s$^{-1}$ at H$\alpha$ are undersampled by the MUSE instrument.

limitations_admitted.value: Artefacts in the H-alpha velocity and dispersion maps arise from minute calibration uncertainties at the scale of a few 10s of km s^-1 and LSF undersampling.

evidence.quote: We also note that the artefacts in both maps are arising from minute calibration uncertainties at the scale of a few 10s of km s$^{-1}$ and to undersampling of the MUSE LSF (see Sect. [3.1](#section:kinematics_stars)).

limitations_admitted.value: Voronoi bins in H II regions are typically smaller than the seeing limit, especially at the blue end of the spectrum.

evidence.quote: We caution that bins located in H ii regions are typically below the seeing limit, especially in the blue end of the spectrum (where PSF sizes range between 0.7 – 0.9 arcsec).

limitations_admitted.value: MUSE mosaic only covers the inner optical disk (R <= 1.1 R_e), which may explain the lower global f_DIG compared to wider-field studies.

evidence.quote: This might be due to the fact that the MUSE data only cover the inner portion of the optical disk ($R \leq 1.1~R_e$).

referee_caveats_inferred: Double-Gaussian decomposition at MUSE spectral resolution (sigma_inst ~ 120 km s^-1 at H-alpha) can suffer from degeneracies when component velocity separations are smaller than the instrumental FWHM.
